title: Alike and Different
theme: Comparison and contrast: words and connectors
objectives: I can name how two things are alike and different using precise verbs and nouns.
I can choose the connector that matches the relationship between two ideas.
I can write a compare-and-contrast paragraph with a clear signal word in each sentence.
I can tell the difference between connectors that show likeness and connectors that show contrast.
rationale: Compare and contrast is the most common structure in sixth-grade informational reading, and students lose points when they cannot signal which relationship they mean. The unit pairs four content words (resemble, differ, counterpart, parallel) with six connectors: two that point to likeness (likewise, similarly), one that reverses an idea (conversely), and three that mark a contrast or a surprise (nevertheless, despite, on the contrary). Students practice choosing the right signal, a skill that carries into argument writing and test items about text structure.

words.def: To look like or be similar to another person or thing.
words.ex: Zoe's handwriting resembles her mother's so closely that teachers sometimes mix them up.
words.ex2: From far away, the cloud resembled a giant sleeping dog.
words.nonExample: A cat and a ladder do not resemble each other.

apps.academic: Fossil shells may resemble modern shells, which helps scientists compare them.
apps.spoken: You really resemble your grandfather when you smile.
apps.writing: Use resemble to say that one thing looks or acts like another; add a detail to show how.

cloze.s: The twins ___ each other so closely that even their teachers wear name tags to tell them apart.

cloze2.s: Your drawing of the dragon ___ the one in the book, right down to the curled tail.

misuse.s: A zebra and a polar bear resemble each other because they look nothing alike.
misuse.why: To resemble is to look like something; looking nothing alike is the opposite.

visual.alt: Two people who look alike beside a mirror.

words.def: To be unlike another person or thing in some way.

senses.def: To disagree with someone about an idea.
senses.example: The two scientists differ about what caused the change.

words.ex: The two paintings differ in color, although the shapes are exactly the same.
words.ex2: In the north, winter days differ from summer days in both length and temperature.
words.nonExample: Two identical coins from the same batch do not differ.

apps.academic: Compare how the two narrators differ in what they notice.
apps.spoken: Our opinions differ, but we can still be friends.
apps.writing: Use differ with in or from: differ in size, differ from the first draft.

cloze.s: Identical twins may look alike, but their personalities often ___ in surprising ways.

cloze2.s: The two maps ___ in one important way: only the second shows the new bridge.

misuse.s: The two jackets differ because they are exactly the same in every way.
misuse.why: To differ is to be unlike; being exactly the same is the opposite.

visual.alt: A blue square next to a red square of the same size.

words.def: A person or thing that has the same role as another in a different place or group.
words.ex: Our principal met her counterpart from the school across town to plan a joint field day.
words.ex2: The goalkeeper's counterpart on the other team stopped every shot.
words.nonExample: Two strangers with completely different jobs are not counterparts.
words.rel: the matching person or thing on the other side

apps.academic: A senator's counterpart in another country may have a different title but a similar job.
apps.spoken: My counterpart on the other team is a fast runner.
apps.writing: Use counterpart when two things fill the same role in different settings.

cloze.s: The ambassador met her ___ from the neighboring country to discuss the shared river.

cloze2.s: Our team's captain shook hands with her ___, the captain of the visiting team.

misuse.s: The captain's counterpart was a stranger who held a completely unrelated job at another company.
misuse.why: A counterpart has the same role as someone else; an unrelated job does not match.

visual.alt: Two people shaking hands in front of a globe.

words.frame: The counterpart of a ___ in a ___ is a ___.

words.def: Matching closely, like two lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet.
words.ex: The two stories have parallel plots: in each, a lonely child finds a hidden friend.
words.ex2: The railroad tracks run parallel to the river for miles.
words.nonExample: Two roads that cross at a corner are not parallel.

apps.academic: In geometry, parallel lines never meet; in literature, parallel plots follow similar paths.
apps.spoken: Our schedules run parallel, so we ride the same bus.
apps.writing: Use parallel to show a close match; add a detail to prove it.

cloze.s: The two girls led ___ lives: both moved at age ten, both learned a new language, and both made friends through music.

cloze2.s: The pencil lines on graph paper are ___, so they never cross no matter how far you draw them.

misuse.s: The parallel lines crossed in the middle and made an X.
misuse.why: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and never cross.

visual.alt: A road with two lanes running side by side.

words.ex: Maya cleaned her room; likewise, Jonah tidied the garage.
words.ex2: Bees need flowers to survive. Likewise, many flowers need bees.
words.nonExample: Likewise is not a good link between two ideas that are opposites.

apps.academic: Use likewise to add a second example that follows the same pattern as the first.
apps.spoken: When someone says nice to meet you, you can answer, 'Likewise.'
apps.writing: Put likewise at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma, to show a second matching example.

cloze.s: When the host said, 'Nice to meet you,' Kai smiled and replied simply, '___.'

cloze2.s: Wolves hunt in packs to catch large animals; ___, orcas work together to trap fish.

misuse.s: Carlos loves loud music. Likewise, Dani hates it and covers her ears.
misuse.why: Likewise signals the same pattern; hating loud music is the opposite of loving it.

words.ex: Frogs breathe partly through their skin; similarly, many salamanders absorb oxygen through theirs.
words.ex2: Mei practiced her violin every day, and her brother similarly spent hours at the piano.
words.nonExample: Similarly cannot introduce an idea that is the opposite of the last one.

apps.academic: Use similarly to show that a second example follows a pattern shown in the first.
apps.spoken: We were dressed similarly without planning it.
apps.writing: Similarly can sit at the start of a sentence or beside a verb.

cloze.s: The two sisters were dressed ___: both wore blue jackets and white sneakers.

cloze2.s: Photocopies of the same page will look ___, down to the smallest mark.

misuse.s: The twins dressed similarly: one wore a snowsuit and the other wore only swim trunks.
misuse.why: Similarly means in almost the same way; a snowsuit and swim trunks are very different.

visual.alt: Two matching shirts side by side.

words.def: Used to introduce an idea that is the opposite of the one before it.
words.ex: Exercise can make you tired in the short run; conversely, it gives you more energy over time.
words.ex2: Most plants need sunlight to grow. Conversely, many mushrooms thrive in dark, damp places.
words.nonExample: Conversely does not fit between two sentences that say the same thing.
words.rel: a signal that flips an idea

apps.academic: Use conversely when the second idea is the reverse of the first, not just different.
apps.spoken: Conversely, if we leave early, we will miss the speech.
apps.writing: Put a comma after conversely when it starts a sentence.

cloze.s: Teachers learn a great deal from their students. ___, students learn from their teachers.

cloze2.s: A fast metabolism burns energy quickly; ___, a slow metabolism burns it more gradually.

misuse.s: The first plan saves money. Conversely, the second plan saves money in exactly the same way.
misuse.why: Conversely introduces the opposite idea; the second plan is the same as the first.

visual.alt: Two boxes facing each other, one holding an idea and the other holding its reverse.

words.frame: ___ is true for ___. Conversely, ___ is true for ___.

words.def: In spite of what was just said; even so.
words.ex: Lena was nervous. She nevertheless walked onto the stage and sang her song.
words.ex2: The trail was steep and muddy. Nevertheless, the hikers reached the top by noon.
words.nonExample: Nevertheless does not connect two ideas that agree with each other.

apps.academic: Use nevertheless to show that a result held even though a problem might have changed it.
apps.spoken: It was late. Nevertheless, we kept going.
apps.writing: Nevertheless can follow a period and a comma, or sit in the middle of a sentence.

cloze.s: The goalie had a sore wrist. ___, she blocked every shot in the final ten minutes.

cloze2.s: The directions were confusing, but the class ___ finished the experiment on time.

misuse.s: It was sunny and warm. Nevertheless, we had a perfect day outside.
misuse.why: Nevertheless signals a surprise or contrast; here the second sentence simply agrees.

visual.alt: A tent standing firm in the rain.

words.def: In spite of; even though something might have stopped it.
words.ex: Despite the heavy snow, the bus arrived on time.
words.ex2: Kai finished the race despite a sore ankle.
words.nonExample: Despite is not used to give the reason that something happened.
words.rel: a signal for something that did not stop an action

apps.academic: Despite is followed by a noun or an -ing phrase, not by a full sentence.
apps.spoken: We went swimming despite the cold.
apps.writing: Use despite to show an obstacle that did not change the result.

cloze.s: ___ the long line, the museum staff moved everyone inside in ten minutes.

cloze2.s: The team celebrated ___ losing the final game, proud of how far they had come.

misuse.s: We stayed home despite the storm because the sky was clear and sunny.
misuse.why: Despite introduces an obstacle that did not stop the action; a clear sky is no obstacle.

visual.alt: A cyclist riding through a storm.

words.def: Used to say that the opposite of what was just said is true.
words.ex: "Was the movie boring?" "On the contrary, I could not look away."
words.ex2: The new rule does not make life harder for students; on the contrary, it saves them time.
words.nonExample: On the contrary does not show that two ideas agree.
words.rel: a signal that corrects an idea

apps.academic: Use on the contrary to correct a wrong idea and then give the truth.
apps.spoken: No, on the contrary, I'm glad you asked.
apps.writing: On the contrary usually follows a sentence that has a negative word such as not.

cloze.s: "Are you upset about the schedule change?" "No, ___, I asked for it."

cloze2.s: The experiment did not fail; ___, it produced the best data we have had so far.

misuse.s: "Is the soup too hot?" "On the contrary, it is far too hot to eat."
misuse.why: On the contrary says the opposite is true; this answer agrees with the question.

visual.alt: A claim with an X over it, and its opposite shown beside it.

words.frame: Some people think ___. On the contrary, ___.

passage.title: Frogs and Toads
paras: At first glance, a frog and a toad resemble each other so closely that many people use the two words as if they meant the same animal. Both are amphibians, which means they begin life in water and, as adults, can live on land. Both have wide mouths, bulging eyes, and strong back legs. Their life stories are parallel: each hatches from an egg laid in water, grows as a tadpole, and then changes into an adult.

Even so, the two animals differ in ways that scientists notice right away. A frog usually has smooth, moist skin and long legs built for leaping. Its counterpart, the toad, tends to have drier, bumpy skin and shorter legs, so it hops or walks instead of jumping far.

Their homes also show a contrast. Most frogs stay close to ponds and streams, where they keep their skin wet. Toads, conversely, can spend more time in drier places, because their thicker skin loses water more slowly.

Young frogs and young toads share another habit. Tadpoles of both kinds breathe with gills. Similarly, the adults of both kinds eat insects and other small animals. Likewise, both groups call out at night, and the sound helps them find mates.

Some people believe that touching a toad causes warts. On the contrary, the bumps on a toad are part of its skin, and handling one does not give a person warts. Nevertheless, it is wise to wash your hands after touching any wild animal. Despite their differences, frogs and toads belong to the same large group of tailless amphibians, and scientists often study them side by side.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "counterpart" refers to
choices: an animal that fills a similar role in a different group
an animal that hunts frogs
a smaller copy of a frog
a place where frogs lay eggs
qs.why: The toad is described as the frog's counterpart because it is the matching animal in the other group.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "conversely" signals that the author will next show
choices: another way that frogs and toads are alike
a reason why frogs live in ponds
a surprise ending to the passage
the opposite of what was just said about frogs
qs.why: The sentence turns from frogs staying near water to toads living in drier places, which is the reverse.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that the life stories of frogs and toads are parallel?
choices: Frogs have smooth skin and toads have bumpy skin.
Toads can live in drier places.
Toads do not cause warts.
Both hatch from eggs in water, grow as tadpoles, and become adults.
qs.why: Parallel means matching closely, and the matching steps of hatching, growing as a tadpole, and changing show it.

qs.q: Why does the author use "On the contrary" in paragraph 5?
choices: To agree with the belief about warts
To compare two kinds of toads
To describe how toads find mates
To correct a belief that is not true
qs.why: The author states a common belief and then says the opposite is true: toads do not cause warts.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Frogs are more useful to people than toads.
Frogs and toads share many traits but also have some general differences.
Toads cause warts, and frogs do not.
All amphibians live only in water.
qs.why: The passage describes both likenesses and differences between two similar animals.

write.prompt: Compare two animals, sports, or places you know well. Use at least four words from this unit, including one that shows likeness and one that shows contrast.
write.frame: A ___ resembles a ___ because ___. Conversely, they differ in ___.

parts.m: like + wise: in the same way
counter + part: the matching piece or role

study.task: Pick two compound words from the unit and explain how each part adds meaning. Then write one sentence for each in which the word links two ideas.

groups.label: showing how things are different or opposite
showing that something held in spite of a problem

choices: agree : disagree
happy : glad
paper : write
bird : nest
also : too
hot : cold
wheel : car
pencil : eraser

sentences: Write a sentence that uses resemble to compare two people, animals, or objects and names one detail that proves it.
Write a sentence that uses differ and names two things that differ in more than one way.
Write a sentence with despite that tells about something a person did even though it was hard.
Write two sentences that use conversely to show opposite results.

combine.model: Maya sang in the concert despite her sore throat.

given: The two animals are opposites in this habit.
combine.model: Cats groom themselves; conversely, dogs need regular baths.

discuss: What is the difference between likewise and conversely? Give one example for each.
When is it better to say nevertheless than despite? Explain with one sentence each.
Two sports can resemble each other in one way and differ in another. Which sports would you compare, and why?
produce.explain: Explain what makes two things parallel and why that is different from simply being similar. Use parallel and a real example.

argue.prompt: Claim: Reading a book is more rewarding than watching its movie version. Take a side and support it with two reasons, using words from this unit to compare the two.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. Reading a book and watching a movie differ in ___. Conversely, ___.

constructed.prompt: Choose two things, such as two games, two seasons, or two pets. Write two sentences that explain how they resemble each other and how they differ.
look: names a real likeness and a real difference
gives a specific detail for each
constructed.model: Soccer and basketball resemble each other because both have two teams that try to score goals. They differ in the ball, the size of the court, and whether players may use their hands.

constructed.prompt: Write a short paragraph with one sentence that uses likewise to add a matching example and one that uses conversely to flip an idea.
constructed.model: Maya recycles her paper at school. Likewise, her brother recycles cans at home. Conversely, their neighbor throws everything in one bin.

constructed.prompt: Write three sentences that use nevertheless, despite, and on the contrary. Each should show a different kind of contrast.
look: each word shows its own kind of contrast
constructed.model: Despite the rain, the game went on. The field was soaked; nevertheless, both teams played hard. No one thought the game was a waste of time; on the contrary, everyone wanted to play again.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words and connectors for comparing and contrasting, practice choosing among them in a short informational passage about frogs and toads, and write their own compare-and-contrast paragraphs. The unit also revisits inverse, proportion, and correspond from the math unit as words that name relationships.

notes.va.resemble.v: Resemble means look like or be similar to. Remind students that it is followed by the thing without a preposition: resembles her mother, not resembles to. Ask for the detail that proves the resemblance.
notes.va.differ.v: Differ in a quality, differ from another thing. Name the second sense, to disagree, but keep the focus on unlike. Students sometimes write differ with where differ from is correct.
notes.va.counterpart.n: Counterpart is the matching person or thing in another group. Use school roles: the captain of each team, the principal of each school. Avoid confusing it with opposite.
notes.va.parallel.adj: Use the math picture of two lines that never meet, then the literature use of parallel plots. Ask for the detail that shows the match. Connect to the math word correspond.
notes.va.likewise.adv: Likewise adds a second matching example. It can also be a polite reply (Likewise). Contrast with however. Have students rewrite a pair of sentences with likewise.
notes.va.similarly.adv: Similarly is a slightly longer cousin of likewise. It can follow a semicolon or start a sentence. Note it can also modify a verb: dressed similarly.
notes.va.conversely.adv: Conversely reverses an idea: the opposite case. Draw two boxes facing each other. Students often use it where however would do; remind them that conversely needs a true reverse.
notes.va.nevertheless.adv: Nevertheless means even so. Break the compound into never + the + less. Have students pair a problem with a result that held anyway. Contrast with despite, which needs a noun phrase.
notes.va.despite.prep: Despite takes a noun or an -ing phrase, not a full sentence. Write both patterns on the board: despite the rain; despite being tired. Ask students to avoid despite of.
notes.va.on-the-contrary.phr: Introduce with a false statement, then correct it: Many people think toads cause warts. On the contrary, they do not. Practice with five false statements about school. It is not just no.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The first sentence says frogs stay near water. The next one says toads can live in drier places. That is the opposite, so conversely fits. If both sentences said the same thing, I would choose likewise or similarly. The connector is a signal for the relationship between ideas.'
discuss: Which connector would you use to start a sentence about two animals that are alike? Why?
How does a connector help a reader predict what comes next?
misconceptions: Likewise and conversely can be swapped.
Despite is followed by a full sentence.
On the contrary just means no.
extend: Find a paragraph in a social studies or science text and underline every comparison signal; sort them into likeness, difference, and surprise.
Write a paragraph that compares two characters from different books using at least four unit words.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the connectors two days later with a sorting task (likeness, contrast, opposite) and at one week with a cloze paragraph that leaves out the connectors. Connect to inverse, proportion, and correspond from the math unit as other words that name relationships.

wida.oral: Partner A names two things and says one way they are alike. Partner B says one way they differ and adds a connector from the unit to link the two ideas.

needsReview: Facts in the passage (frogs and toads): both are amphibians that begin as tadpoles with gills; frogs usually have smooth, moist skin and toads drier, bumpy skin; toads' thicker skin loses water more slowly; adults of both eat insects and small animals; both call at night to attract mates; touching toads does not cause warts; both belong to the same large order of tailless amphibians. These are standard but should be checked by a science teacher.

Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: parecerse a, ser diferente (diferir can also mean postpone in Spanish), homólogo, igualmente, de manera similar, a la inversa, sin embargo, a pesar de, al contrario.

likewise has a polite-reply use (Likewise) in cloze 1, which is the only item where similarly would not fit; cloze items for the other connectors can be answered by more than one connector in isolation, so the sense is decided by the wider sentence.
Compound segmentation of nevertheless (never + the + less) is a teaching gloss, not a claim about history.
